item.title: About the Project
item.description:
The Wild West Hypothesis

In a stable market, any obvious and easily exploitable opportunity will eventually be discovered and pursued. Competition gradually erodes these opportunities, making it increasingly difficult to maintain an advantage. As a result, the optimal strategy is to develop a relative advantage by investing heavily in becoming exceptionally good at a specific niche.

In a rapidly changing market, however, opportunities constantly emerge and disappear. The competitive landscape is less predictable, and established advantages can quickly become obsolete. In this environment, the optimal strategy shifts from dominating an established niche to continuously identifying and pursuing new opportunities.

item.title: Blindspot
item.description:
What it does

Blindspot is the scout of the Wild West project. You give it a broad subject — say, home caregiving or ESP32 development — and it mines public online communities for the questions people keep asking. It returns a ranked shortlist of recurring problems, each graded on how worthwhile it would be to build a tool for it.

The point is to choose problems by what people are actively asking for, not by what I happen to find interesting.

item.title: ESP32 Compatibility Table
item.description:
The problem

A new major version of the ESP32 Arduino core (4.0) was released on 19 November 2026. Nobody knows yet which of the thousands of community libraries — for sensors, displays, networking, LEDs and motors — still work with it.

Last time this happened, moving from 2.x to 3.x in 2024, many libraries broke. It took the community months of scattered forum posts and GitHub issues to work out what still worked. Version 4.0 is built on ESP-IDF 6, which removed legacy drivers, treats compiler warnings as errors and changed the crypto API, so a similar wave of breakage is likely. Espressif officially tests about 10 libraries. Everything else is untested.
